name: Aglianico

lines.s10: Aglianico is the slow, dark red of southern Italy's mountains: black cherry, tar and smoke on a tannin that takes years to soften.
lines.s20: Aglianico makes Taurasi in Campania and Aglianico del Vulture in Basilicata, mountain reds of the south. It brings black cherry, tar and smoke, with high acidity and a firm tannin that wants a decanter, a braise or ten years.
lines.s45: Aglianico is southern Italy's mountain red, the grape of Taurasi in the hills of Campania and of Vulture, an extinct volcano in Basilicata. It tastes of black cherry and black plum, with tar, leather and a smoky edge. It is full bodied, with high acidity and firm, drying tannin. Taurasi rests three years before release, at least one in wood, in large old casks or small new barrels that add vanilla. Australia and California grow a little, riper and rounder. Pour it with roast lamb, braised goat or aged hard cheese. In the high vineyards it is picked in November, sometimes after the first snow on the peaks.
lines.sale: Aglianico is a southern red with a mountain freshness: dark cherry and smoke, lifted by high acidity, with a grip that roast meat softens. Give the Taurasi an hour of air and bring it with the lamb.

glass.lead: Black cherry, black plum and dried fig over tar, leather and smoke, on a full body with high acidity and a firm, drying tannin.

ladder.where: The high hills of Irpinia and the slopes of Monte Vulture
The lower Sannio, McLaren Vale, the Riverland and Paso Robles

glass.structure: Dry. Acidity high, tannin high and drying, alcohol medium plus, body full; deep ruby, turning garnet at the rim early.

home.home: Campania and Basilicata. In Campania it makes Taurasi in the high, cold hills of Irpinia, at least 85 per cent Aglianico and three years in the cellar, and Aglianico del Taburno near Benevento. In Basilicata it is Aglianico del Vulture, from the ash and tuff of an extinct volcano.
home.abroad: Australia grows a little, in McLaren Vale, the Riverland and Heathcote, and so does Paso Robles in California; these wines tend to be riper and rounder, the acidity still bright.

service.temp: 61 to 64 degrees Fahrenheit, 16 to 18 degrees Celsius, a cool room temperature.
service.glass: A tall Bordeaux glass, with room to swirl.
service.decant: Yes for a young Taurasi or Vulture, after a taste; an older bottle gently, to leave its sediment.
service.age: Taurasi and Vulture Superiore ten to twenty five years; younger Irpinia Aglianico usually within five.

with.why: fat and protein soften the firm grip
acidity meets the tomato, tannin the meat

with.dish: Pasta with a long cooked meat ragù
with.why: a rich sauce for a wine of high acidity
salt and fat round off the tannin

labels.means: Aglianico from the hills of Irpinia in Campania, at least 85 per cent, aged three years with one in wood.
Basilicata's Aglianico from Monte Vulture; Superiore is the DOCG tier, wholly Aglianico and aged three years.
Aglianico from the Taburno massif near Benevento, at least 85 per cent; a DOCG since 2011.
Younger Aglianico from the Taurasi communes, released sooner under the wider Irpinia DOC.
Longer ageing: four years for Taurasi with eighteen months in wood, five for Vulture Superiore.

guest.q: Why do people call it the Barolo of the South?
guest.a: For its structure: high acidity and a firm tannin that want years, as Nebbiolo does. The taste differs, deeper in colour, with black cherry and smoke where Barolo shows rose petal and red cherry.

guest.q: Is Taurasi the same wine as Aglianico del Vulture?
guest.a: The same grape from two regions. Taurasi grows in the hills of Campania on clay and limestone with volcanic layers; Vulture grows on the ash and tuff of an extinct volcano in Basilicata.

guest.q: Will it be too tannic for tonight?
guest.a: A young one grips. An hour in a decanter and a rich dish of lamb or a slow ragù settle it; a bottle ten years old has already softened.

compare.tell: Nebbiolo is paler, with rose petal and red cherry; Aglianico is deeper in colour and darker in fruit, with black cherry, black plum and smoke.
Sagrantino is blacker and grips even harder, with blackberry, cocoa and dried violet; Aglianico carries more acidity and a smoky, iron edge.
Nero d'Avola is softer and rounder, ripe plum and black cherry with gentle tannin; Aglianico grips harder, with higher acidity, tar and smoke.

cards.front: Aglianico: which two southern wines does it make, and in which regions?
cards.back: Taurasi, in the hills of Irpinia in Campania, and Aglianico del Vulture, on an extinct volcano in Basilicata. Aglianico del Taburno, near Benevento, is a third.

cards.front: Taurasi: how much Aglianico must it hold, and how long before release?
cards.back: At least 85 per cent Aglianico, aged three years with at least one in wood. The Riserva ages four years, eighteen months of them in wood.

cards.front: Why is Aglianico picked so late, and when does its harvest fall?
cards.back: It buds early and ripens late, and its hard tannin needs the whole season. In Irpinia and on Vulture the harvest runs into late October and November.

questions.q: A red poured blind is deep ruby, with black cherry, tar and smoke, high acidity and a firm, drying tannin. The guest says it is from southern Italy. Which grape is it?
questions.exp: High acidity with a hard, drying tannin, tar and smoke point to Aglianico. Nero d'Avola, the nearest miss, is softer and rounder, with ripe black cherry and gentler tannin.

questions.q: A guest who loves Taurasi asks for the same grape from another region, grown on the slopes of an extinct volcano. Which wine do you bring?
questions.exp: Aglianico del Vulture is Aglianico from Monte Vulture in Basilicata. Etna Rosso, the nearest miss, is volcanic too but is Nerello Mascalese, from an active volcano in Sicily.

questions.q: A table has ordered slow roasted lamb and asks for a southern Italian red with the grip to meet it. Which bottle do you bring?
questions.exp: Taurasi is Aglianico, with high acidity and a firm, drying tannin that the lamb's fat and protein soften. Frappato, the nearest miss, is pale, light and soft in tannin.

report: Mode home, as the plan fixes it. Nothing contradicts TASTE.world old.

The rules (Taurasi at least 85 per cent, three years with one in wood, Riserva four with eighteen months; Aglianico del Taburno a DOCG of 2011; Aglianico del Vulture DOC 1971 and its Superiore DOCG of 2010, wholly Aglianico, three years, Riserva five), the Campi Taurasini sub zone, the late harvest into November with snow on the peaks, the large old casks against barrique, and lamb, braised goat and aged caciocavallo all stand on the Codex's Campania and Calabria and Basilicata records.

Abroad: McLaren Vale, the Riverland and Heathcote stand on Wine Companion and Decanter as search results quoted them; Paso Robles on three trade pages read the same way. The hosts could not be opened in this session, so a checker should open them.

Colour: GRAPES calls Aglianico deep ruby garnet, while the Codex's Campania trap says it is pale next to Montepulciano and warns against reading its garnet rim as age. The entry says deep ruby, turning garnet at the rim early, which both records allow.
Acidity: GRAPES and INTRO_GRAPES say high and TASTE says medium plus (acid 2); the structure line follows the reviewed profile and says high. Alcohol follows TASTE, medium plus.
The name's origin (the old reading as Hellenic, Greek) is left out: it is disputed and the sources at hand do not settle it.
